title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
hook: eyes, nose, mouth, tongue, skin: the classical morning wakes the senses one by one

segments.voice: Yesterday the daily routine began before sunrise: rise in brahma muhurta to protect life, and ask the body first.

Lay the classical texts' morning care side by side and it covers a lot of ground in a small space: a tour of the face, eyes, nose, teeth, tongue and mouth, and then the skin, all of it. Read quickly, it's a hygiene checklist. Read slowly, it's a way of waking the senses up one at a time, so the person who walks out the door has actually arrived in their own body. It's also the end of the week, so a look back comes after.
screen: `EYES, NOSE, TEETH, TONGUE.` → `A TOUR OF THE FACE.` → `THE SENSES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita and the Ashtanga Hridaya both walk through this morning care, each in its own order. Paraphrased: the eyes are tended. The teeth are cleaned with a twig, chewed into a soft brush. The tongue is scraped. The mouth is rinsed and gargled, sometimes with oil. Drops of oil may go in the nose. Then oil for the body, and a bath. Each of these is a door. The eyes see, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the skin feels. And in Hindu thought the senses matter far beyond hygiene. The Gita, for one, pictures a steady person drawing the senses in, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. The morning round doesn't preach about any of that. It just touches each door, gently, before the day starts knocking on all of them, from the head down, from small to whole: a twig for the teeth before oil for the whole body. Now the week. The doshas took their turns on the clock, stacked like on like, split into nature and today, and closed on health as the three in balance. Then the daily round opened: dina, day, charya, conduct. It rose before sunrise, in the verse at least, to protect life, and checked in with the body first. And today, the senses, woken one by one. The thread through all of it: Ayurveda keeps building health out of ordinary minutes.
screen: `EYES, TEETH, TONGUE, MOUTH, SKIN` · `EACH SENSE IS A DOOR` · `FROM THE HEAD DOWN, SMALL TO WHOLE` · `THE WEEK: ORDINARY MINUTES`

segments.voice: Without moving, soften the eyes and notice light and shape, then the nearest sound and the farthest. Then the air and any smell at all, the taste of your mouth right now, and the skin: clothes, air, the weight where you sit. Door by door, then let them rest together in the breath; if you pray, you can name each sense as a gift as you pass it.
The daily routine. In the classical morning, eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth and skin are each tended in turn, waking the senses one by one.
Your line: the daily routine, dinacharya. Each sense is a door. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five, done.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda's morning round tend the eyes, clean the teeth, scrape the tongue, rinse or gargle the mouth, and some use oil in the nose or on the body before bathing.

original.note: Sanskrit indriya: a sense, or sense faculty, in Ayurveda and in the Upanishads and the Gita.

trapdoor: what you thought: morning care is a hygiene checklist.
what it means: the daily round tends each sense, eyes, teeth, tongue, mouth, skin, waking the person into the body.
what a scholar hears: indriya, the senses, a word Ayurveda shares with the Upanishads and the Gita, where the senses are gathered in.

chat.says: Why do the old texts care so much about scraping tongues and tending eyes?
options: Each is a door for a sense; the morning round wakes them gently, one by one.
Just for looking good: the texts say the senses don't matter beyond hygiene.
Because a sick person must finish every step of it before eating at all.
chat.meaning: Eyes, nose, tongue and skin are doors for the senses. The classical morning care tends each in turn, waking them one by one.

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

charya.meaning: a way of going about, a conduct

brahma muhurta.meaning: the time before sunrise, set apart in Hindu tradition

Ashtanga Hridaya.meaning: a classical Ayurveda text, the heart of eight branches

recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
